You place moments in time with “als” (once, in the past) and “wenn” (every time / in the future), you ask with “wann?”, and you start the sentence with the subordinate clause (Als ich klein war, …).
when (a single time, in the past)
when (every time; in the present / future); if
to take off, to leave (by plane)
When I was little, I lived in Sibiu.
When I get home, I'll call you.
Every time I eat honey, I think of my dad.
When we landed, it was raining.
Use “als” for a single moment in the past (Als ich zehn war…).
Use “wenn” for repeated actions (in the past too) and for the present / future.
Use “wann” only in questions (direct and indirect).
Start the sentence with the subordinate clause: then the main clause begins with the VERB (Wenn ich komme, rufe ich an).
Recognise the Präteritum of common verbs in written stories (wohnte, regnete, kam, ging).
It's August. Mara and Lena are flying from Berlin to Sibiu. It's Lena's first time in Romania and she has lots of questions.
In forty minutes. If the weather's good, you'll see the Carpathians straight away.
I'm so nervous. What happens if your parents don't like me?
Lena! Mum has been cooking for three days. When she cooks for three days for someone, it means she already likes them.
And Andrei? Will he be at the airport?
Yes. He wrote to me: “When you land, I'll be there with flowers.” Flowers! He's never bought me flowers.
Tell me about Sibiu. What was it like when you were little?

When I was little, the old town was still grey and run-down. But in 2007 Sibiu was European Capital of Culture, and then everything was renovated. When I saw it for the first time, I was ten. I almost didn't recognise the town.
And what did you do when you were homesick? In Berlin, I mean.
Every time I was homesick, I opened a jar of my dad's honey. One teaspoon of honey, and I was home again.
That's why you've got three jars of honey in the cupboard!
There are only two left now. The winter in Berlin was long. Look! Down there! The mountains!
“wann” = “vahn” (a), “wenn” = “ven” (e). The difference is a single vowel, but the meaning is different!
“Heimweh” = “HIME-vay”: ei = “eye”, and the h after e isn't pronounced.
“als” = when, for a SINGLE moment or a SINGLE period in the past. It's a subordinating conjunction: the verb goes to the end.
When I was little, I lived in Sibiu. (childhood = a single period)
When we landed, it was raining. (once)
When I saw the town, I was ten.
repeated actions in the past (every time)
Immer wenn ich Heimweh hatte, aß ich Honig.
Every time I was homesick, I ate honey.
Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.
When it rains, I stay at home.
Wenn ihr landet, stehe ich da.
When you land, I'll be there.
Wenn das Wetter gut ist, siehst du die Berge.
If the weather's good, you'll see the mountains.
Trick for the past: if you can add “every time”, it's “wenn”. If it happened only once, it's “als”.
Do you know when we land? (indirect question, verb at the end)
A typical mistake for English speakers, since English has just one word, “when”: “Wann ich klein war…” Correct: “Als ich klein war…”.
4. The subordinate clause in first place
If the sentence begins with the subordinate clause, it takes POSITION 1. The main clause starts directly with the VERB (position 2), then the subject:
The result: two verbs side by side, separated by a comma: “…komme, rufe…”. That's the sign you've built the sentence correctly.
In written stories (books, articles), German uses the Präteritum, not the Perfekt. For now you only need to RECOGNISE it:
Regular verbs take “-te” (wohnte, spielte). Irregular ones change their vowel (kam, ging, sah). In the coming chapters you'll meet them more and more often in the stories.
Do you know when the train is coming?
___ ich 2015 in Wien war, habe ich Ludwig kennengelernt.
___ ich in Wien war, habe ich immer Sachertorte gegessen.
Wenn ich Zeit habe, ich komme.
Wenn ich Zeit habe, komme ich.
Wenn ich habe Zeit, komme ich.
When you land, I'll be there with flowers.
When I was a child, I had a dog.
When I have time, I read.
Sie hat Angst, dass Maras Eltern sie nicht mögen.
Was hat Mara gemacht, wenn sie Heimweh hatte?

When the plane landed in Sibiu, the sun was shining. The airport was small, much smaller than in Berlin, and after ten minutes Mara and Lena were already standing with their suitcases in the arrivals hall. Andrei was there, as he'd promised, with a huge bunch of sunflowers. He gave Mara a kiss on the cheek and Lena the flowers. Then he went as red as the suitcases.
Welcome to Sibiu, Lena! I'm so glad!
Just a little. I had a good teacher. On the phone.

Mara's parents lived in an old house in the Lower Town, with thick walls, a green gate and a big garden behind the house. When they arrived, Mara's mother was already standing in the doorway. She hugged Mara for a long time without saying anything. Then she hugged Lena just as long, as if she had known her for years, and said in German, which she had secretly learned with an app: “Welcome. You are very thin. Come and eat.”

And Lena ate. She ate ciorbă, a sour vegetable soup, she ate sarmale, which were even better than Mara's Berlin sarmale, she ate mămăligă (polenta) with cheese and sour cream, and at the end she ate papanași, big warm doughnuts with jam and sour cream. When she wanted to refuse the third one, Mara's mother looked at her so sadly that she took it after all.

After the meal, Mara's father showed Lena the bees. He was a quiet man with big hands who spoke little, neither German nor much English. But when he opened the first hive and took out the honeycombs, golden and heavy, Lena understood every word he didn't say. She was a baker. She knew what it means to get up early every day and make something with your hands.
Mara says you make the best bread in Berlin. If you get up early tomorrow, we'll bake together. With my honey.

Mara translated. Lena nodded enthusiastically. The next morning at five they were standing together in the kitchen, the silent beekeeper and the Berlin baker, with no common language but with flour up to their elbows. When Mara woke up at eight, the whole house smelled of honey bread.

Over the following days Mara showed Lena the town. The Great Square with its colourful houses, the Bridge of Lies, where, as the legend says, you mustn't lie, or it collapses. And the roofs. Lena stopped in the middle of the square and looked up.
The houses are looking at me! Andrei was right. The roofs have eyes.
When I was little, I was afraid of them. I thought they saw everything I did. Every time I wanted to do something forbidden, I looked up first.

On the third day they went to Rășinari, the village of Mara's grandparents, twelve kilometres from the town, at the foot of the mountains. Her grandmother was eighty and so small that she only came up to Lena's shoulder. When she heard that Lena was a baker, she immediately took her by the hand and led her to the summer kitchen behind the house, where there was an old wood-fired oven. An hour later they both came out with red cheeks and a round loaf that smelled of smoke and caraway. Grandma didn't speak a word of German, and Lena didn't speak a word of Romanian. “How did you understand each other?” Mara asked. Lena shrugged: “With our hands. Dough is the same everywhere.”

That evening Andrei and Lena walked alone along the old city wall as the sun was setting behind the mountains. Mara stayed at home and helped her mother with the washing-up. Her mother asked, just in passing: “This Lena… isn't she a bit old for Andrei?” Mara smiled: “Nine years, Mum. Dad is seven years older than you.” Her mother said nothing more. But the next morning she put the best jar of honey next to Lena's plate.

On the fourth day, just as they were standing on the Bridge of Lies, Mara's phone rang. An email from the Goethe-Institut. Subject: “Your exam result”. Mara went pale. Her hands were shaking so badly that Lena had to take the phone.
Reading: 88 per cent. Listening: 79 per cent. Writing: 92 per cent. Speaking: 95 per cent. Mara. Mara! You passed! With “very good” in speaking!

Mara said nothing. She stood in the middle of the Bridge of Lies and cried. Andrei hugged her. Lena hugged them both. A few tourists looked at them and took photos, because they thought it was a tradition.

When she had calmed down a little, Mara immediately rang Berlin. Not her mother, who lived two streets away and would find out in ten minutes anyway, but an old man in a first-floor flat, under a yellow lamp.
Ludwig? I passed. I did it!

At the other end there was a moment's silence. Then Mara heard Ludwig shout loudly: “Fritz! She passed! Our Mara passed!” And then, in the background, an excited bark. Mara stood on a bridge where you mustn't lie and thought that at that moment she had two places she could call home. And that this wasn't a problem but a stroke of luck. Above her, on the roofs of the old town, the little windows were watching, as always. This time she wasn't afraid of them.
